strengths: Novel problem formulation extending classical social learning with precision control by a central planner, well-motivated by timely applications (targeted ads, persuasive LLMs)

Strong theoretical contribution with complete characterization of optimal altruistic planner policy (Theorems 1, 2, 4); Theorem 2 on convexity of value function is technically non-trivial with creative inductive proof
Important empirical finding that heavily constrained planners can achieve dramatic welfare effects (±26% to ±97%), suggesting significant practical implications
Clear exposition with good intuitive explanations of formal results and well-chosen motivating examples illustrating both benevolent and harmful planner objectives
Rigorous mathematical framework properly formulating the optimization problems as MDPs with well-defined state spaces and transition dynamics
weaknesses: Incomplete characterization of biased planner—Theorem 7 only provides bounds (e.g., region C: π*_B(b) ∈ [1-b, p]) rather than exact optimal policy; this asymmetry significantly weakens the contribution for the equally important biased case

Severely limited experimental evaluation: only ~125,000 total trajectories across all parameter combinations; single instantiation shown in Figure 2 without systematic sensitivity analysis; no statistical testing, confidence intervals, or comparison with alternative control mechanisms

Key theoretical proofs only sketched in main text (especially Theorem 2 on convexity)—full rigorous proofs relegated to supplementary material is problematic for verification and reproducibility of main claims

Highly restrictive model assumptions (binary state/actions, predetermined sequential order, symmetric signals, perfect Bayesian rationality) severely limit applicability to realistic social learning scenarios with continuous choices or heterogeneous agents

Weak practical implications—paper identifies that biased planners cause harm but offers no concrete mitigation strategies, regulatory mechanisms, or institutional designs to address manipulation, only stating this is 'future work'
No ablation studies or comparison with alternative control mechanisms (e.g., monetary incentives vs. information control) to validate the importance of the proposed approach
Limited analysis of how planners interact with information cascades, a central phenomenon in classical social learning; no robustness analysis if model assumptions violated

strengths: Novel problem formulation combining classical social learning with precision control via dynamic programming; planner influence through information precision is a fresh angle on information design

Strong theoretical contributions for altruistic planner: Theorem 2 (convexity of value function) uses technically involved inductive argument over decision trees; Theorem 4 provides complete characterization with clean three-phase threshold structure
Well-motivated applications (targeted ads, political campaigns, LLMs) effectively illustrate practical relevance and ground the research
Systematic treatment: clear separation of myopic vs. optimal cases and careful comparison of altruistic vs. biased objectives
Generally clear writing with good intuitions for main results; structured presentation facilitates understanding
weaknesses: Highly restrictive model assumptions severely limit practical applicability: binary state/action/signal space, symmetric signals by design (contradicts typical manipulation scenarios like selective information provision), fully observable planner control (all agents know all precision choices), and planner has identical information to agents. These appear chosen for mathematical tractability rather than modeling realistic scenarios.

Incomplete characterization of the biased/manipulation case (arguably the more interesting one): Theorem 7 uses bounds like π_B*(b) ∈ [1-b, p] rather than exact characterizations; substantially weakens claims about planner manipulation capabilities

Very weak empirical evaluation: purely simulation-based with no real-world validation or data; narrow parameter exploration (only varies k, p, δ); single detailed example (Figure 2); no sensitivity analysis or robustness to different cost functions; claims about '97% welfare change' lack context about realistic parameter ranges

Underdeveloped practical and ethical implications: abstract promises 'practical policy questions' but delivers little; paper ends with 'future exploration' of safeguards without any concrete analysis of countermeasures, transparency requirements, or regulatory approaches; insufficient for a top-tier venue

Limited engagement with related literature: information design literature (Kamenica-Gentzkow and others) not discussed despite direct relevance; algorithmic persuasion/manipulation literature barely mentioned; distinction from [20] (precision vs. direct payments) feels narrow and not well-justified; gaps in behavioral economics

Proof presentation issues undermine verification: Theorem 2 proof sketch is ~1 paragraph and cannot be verified; decision tree argument needs substantial elaboration; Equation 5 appears without derivation; key results relegated to unprovided reference [25]; insufficient rigor for submission to technical venue
Massive ~80% gap between myopic and optimal altruistic policies suggests myopic analysis is not useful; raises questions about whether myopic characterization adds meaningful insight

Symmetric signal restriction is unjustified: real manipulation involves asymmetric information provision (showing only positive reviews, filtering); assumption that P(s_i = ω) = q_i conflicts with realistic manipulation scenarios; acknowledged but not adequately justified

Incomplete analysis of information cascades: cascade phenomenon is central to social learning literature but treated superficially; limited analysis of when/why cascades occur under different planner policies

Core finding (information control enables manipulation) is somewhat expected and lacks surprising insights; framing about 'dramatic influence' appears overstated given model restrictions; unclear what practitioners should do with theoretical results
Theorem 8 (Precision Monotonicity) feels tautological—stating that better information improves welfare adds little insight and should be a lemma, not a main result

Missing real-world validation, experimental evidence, or data; no comparison to information design frameworks or strategic agent responses; no analysis of detectability or robustness to revealed manipulation

strengths: Novel problem formulation combining sequential social learning with precision investment control, genuinely new to the social learning literature
Rigorous theoretical contributions including non-trivial proof of value function convexity (Theorem 2) with novel techniques, and complete characterization of optimal altruistic policies (Theorem 4)
Compelling and timely real-world applications (targeted ads, political campaigns, persuasive LLMs) that motivate the research
Important negative results: demonstrates that even severely constrained planners (equivalent information, symmetric signals, observable control) can dramatically influence social welfare (±26-97%)
Comprehensive treatment of both altruistic and biased planners under myopic and non-myopic settings with clear policy structures
weaknesses: Incomplete theoretical characterization: optimal biased policy is only bounded in regions (C) and (D) of Theorem 7, whereas altruistic policy is fully characterized; conditions determining thresholds t₁ and t₂ not fully specified

Limited empirical evaluation: only one cost function family tested (linear), single discount factor δ=0.75 shown in figures, no robustness analysis across cost function assumptions, no confidence intervals despite averaging 1000 trajectories

Key theoretical proof (Theorem 2 on value function convexity) provided only as sketch in main paper due to space constraints, requiring readers to reference [25] for verification of most technically involved result

No proposed solutions to the identified manipulation problem; paper identifies significant threat to social learning but provides no concrete defense mechanisms, mitigation strategies, or policy implications

Restrictive model assumptions (binary state/actions, sequential predetermined order, Bayesian rational agents) limit generalizability; unclear how insights extend to continuous choices, multi-outcome settings, or non-sequential decision processes

strengths: Novel framework integrating algorithmic control with sequential social learning, addressing an important and timely problem in AI governance
Non-trivial theoretical contributions, particularly Theorem 2 proving convexity of the altruistic value function using sophisticated decision-tree arguments
Comprehensive characterization of optimal policies for both altruistic and biased planners under transparent constraints (no lying, no censoring)
Sophisticated LLM-based empirical validation demonstrating emergent strategic behavior and identifying systematic non-Bayesian deviations (NB1-NB3)
Concrete quantification of welfare impacts (40-50% reductions with biased planners), demonstrating substantial real-world significance
Well-motivated examples and clear articulation of why algorithmic information control + social learning interaction matters for AI policy
weaknesses: Highly restrictive modeling assumptions: binary states/signals, homogeneous agents, complete information parity between planner and agents limits applicability beyond proof-of-concept

Significant theory-practice gap: optimal policies characterized for Bayesian agents, but empirical validation reveals non-Bayesian LLM behavior; limited guidance on designing systems for actual non-Bayesian agents

Incomplete characterization of biased planner (Theorem 5): optimal policies may not exist in some regions (region E), and intuition for different policy modes (obfuscation, investment patterns) could be clearer

Limited empirical validation: single domain (car purchasing), one LLM model tested, experiments on only 10 agents, no human subjects or real-world deployment data, artificial oracle approach for message generation
Inadequate treatment of interventions: paper identifies the problem but offers minimal concrete solutions for preventing harmful steering or operationalizing theoretical insights for practitioners
Scalability concerns: experiments on small scales; unclear how results generalize to large heterogeneous populations, multiple competing planners, or network settings
Presentation: dense notation and heavy reliance on appendices for proofs reduces accessibility; key intuitions could be foregrounded before formal results

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing algorithmic information mediation and LLM influence on social learning
Rigorous theoretical analysis with formal characterization of optimal policies for both altruistic and biased planners
Novel proof of value function convexity using decision tree induction
Integration of LLM-based experiments alongside theoretical analysis
Clear acknowledgment of model limitations and explicit statement of assumptions
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice disconnect: theory assumes Bayesian agents but experiments demonstrate LLMs are systematically non-Bayesian (NB1-NB3), undermining claimed empirical validation
Oversimplified model with binary state/signal spaces that may not generalize; unclear whether results transfer to realistic continuous or multidimensional settings
Insufficient empirical validation: single LLM model, single application domain, no real-world data, no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals
Policy characterization theorems lack interpretability—optimal policies characterized through abstract threshold parameters (dA, tA, etc.) with limited economic intuition
Welfare analysis is superficial: striking claim of 40-50% welfare loss under biased control only demonstrated in simulation with no theoretical characterization or proposed remedies
Unrealistic modeling assumptions: binary symmetric signals, planner has exact same information as agents, full observability of control choices
Limited technical novelty: techniques are standard MDP methods; main contribution is problem formulation rather than methodological advance
Incomplete practical guidance: no implementation guidance, computational complexity analysis, parameter estimation procedures, or concrete regulatory recommendations
Narrow scope: biased planner restricted to single preferred action; heterogeneous preferences only briefly sketched in appendix; multi-planner settings not considered
Insufficient engagement with related work: minimal differentiation from Bayesian persuasion literature and limited discussion of what specifically extends prior work

strengths: Novel framework combining information design with sequential social learning, addressing an important and timely problem at the intersection of algorithmic mediation and social dynamics
Non-trivial theoretical contributions, especially Theorem 2 (value function convexity), whose proof sophisticatedly handles unusual belief update structure and agent action dependencies
Rigorous characterization of optimal planner policies (Theorems 3, 5) providing actionable insights about when and how planners should invest in signal precision

Effective bridge between theory and practice: LLM simulations identify specific non-Bayesian behaviors (NB1-NB3) and demonstrate that LLM planner strategies align with theoretical predictions despite agent irrationality
Respects important transparency constraints: no falsification, information parity, full observability, making the model more realistic than unrestricted information design
Clear practical relevance: demonstrates biased planners can reduce social welfare by 40-50% through information obscuration, with concrete policy implications
Well-written and well-organized presentation with strong motivation and clear intuitive examples before formal treatment
weaknesses: Highly restrictive modeling assumptions limit applicability: binary state space, binary symmetric signals, and homogeneous agent preferences (heterogeneous preferences unresolved for biased planner case)
Incomplete theoretical results: biased planner analysis yields ϵ-optimal policies in some belief ranges rather than true optimality (Theorem 5 part E), limiting practical application

Limited experimental evaluation: single domain tested (car-buying), single LLM model (LG AI EXAONE 32B), no statistical reporting (confidence intervals, sample sizes), limited ablations, and no comparison with alternative information design approaches

Information cascades are central to social learning but receive minimal analysis; no discussion of convergence properties, equilibrium beliefs, or planner strategies for deliberately triggering cascades

Artificial oracle setup in experiments: LLMs do not directly optimize over precision space but rely on an external 'belief oracle,' reducing authenticity and limiting insights about emergent LLM behavior
Practical applicability gaps: assumes planner observes all actions and signal precisions are observable; provides no guidance on estimating cost function β(·) in real systems

Paper identifies welfare harms from biased planners but proposes no concrete mitigation mechanisms beyond vague mention of 'regulations or mechanisms' in conclusion; significant gap between diagnosis and remedy
